records.name: Réunion
records.summary:
French equality law applies in full as an overseas department: same-sex marriage reached the island with the metropolitan statute (2013), 'sexual identity' has been a prosecutable discrimination ground in the penal code since 2012, and the national amendments that produced simplified legal gender change apply here as state law. No offence attaches to being trans, and the protection framework is actionable rather than nominal.

The audited record is honest about its thinness for this island specifically: the only territory-tied adverse documentation is framework-wide — the national detention-places watchdog found serious, persistent violations against transgender prisoners, and investigative reporting details the procedural cracks trans women prisoners fall through — both applying to the island's prisons. No local violence series, enforcement pattern, or institutional hostility programme appears in the sources, and equally no documented local support infrastructure; a small, discreet community should be assumed but is not evidenced.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018, French context): trans women in France incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal gray area - relevant to Réunion as a French overseas department applying French law.

CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (French context, applicable in Réunion): serious violations persist across places of detention.
PinkNews (Aug 2012): France's same-sex marriage bill (marriage and adoption) to be introduced in October - the legislation that extended marriage equality to Réunion as French law.
Yagg (July 2012, in French): 'sexual identity' became a discrimination ground in the French Penal Code (Article L225-1) - enabling prosecution of transphobia; French law applies in Réunion.

Yagg (May 2016, in French): the National Assembly adopted amendment 282 facilitating legal gender change for trans people - though its scope could be limited by three government sub-amendments; French law applies in Réunion.

records.name: Romania
records.summary:
Romania is broadly workable with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark EU court ruling and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Romania must recognize gender-identity changes made in other EU member states (the Mirin case), and a Romanian court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. Bucharest Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the Orthodox Church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

For a visitor: EU/Schengen, no trans-specific border friction, no criminalisation, bathrooms unrestricted. The ECJ ruling means EU-issued LGR documents must be recognised.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Oct 2024) covers the CJEU ruling that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights (the Mirzarafie-Ahi case on recognition of UK gender recognition).

ACCEPT Romania (March 2026): definitive victory in Arian's case - the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ruled (now final after appeals were rejected) that the Romanian state must issue Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi a new birth certificate reflecting the gender identity already recognised in Great Britain before Brexit, following the 2024 CJEU ruling establishing the obligation.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Romania: anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the presidential campaign (Georgescu 'against LGBTQ'; PM Ciolacu's 'skirt' remarks); ACCEPT's complaint led to a public warning to B1 TV for defamatory Pride coverage; a far-right Deputy Mayor vowed never to accept an LGBTI event in Ploiești; misinformation followed the EU LGBTI Equality Strategy 2026-2030.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Romania: the CNCD investigated printing houses refusing LGBT-related print jobs; MP Simion blamed LGBTQI people for weather as divine punishment; 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should have legal recognition (IPSOS PRIDE 2023); new Education Law proposals included diversity obligations, opposed by 13 religious groups; a new Fiscal Code threatens associations' ability to distribute services.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): anti-discrimination ordinance since 2000 but limited institutional progress; no same-sex marriage/civil unions (the Orthodox Church a key opponent; 2018 referendum failed on turnout); the ECtHR ruled in May 2023 that Romania's ban on same-sex unions violates Article 8, but the government has defied the ruling; legal gender change possible but inaccessible, inconsistent and requires surgical intervention.

Council of Europe thematic review (Jan 2023): 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania' - national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering legal/policy frameworks, applicable ECtHR case-law and international standards.

ILGA-Europe and partner organisations' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report - targeted stakeholder consultation covering horizontal developments and country chapters (Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Spain).
AP (Jun 2025): 'Bucharest gay pride march turns 20 as LGBTQ+ Romanians face growing hostility' — tens of thousands march on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.

FRA legal study (Feb 2008) by Iordache & Ionescu: 'Legal Study on Homophobia and Discrimination on Grounds of Sexual Orientation - Romania' - implementation of Employment Directive 2000/78/EC, the NCCD's work, freedom of movement, asylum, family reunification, and freedom of assembly including cases of refusals or bans.

records.name: Russia
records.summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and the US State Department explicitly warns LGBT travellers of this.

The UK Home Office assesses that trans people specifically are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution in Russia. Enforcement has produced over a hundred "extremism" convictions for displaying LGBT symbols or participation, bar raids, and the death in custody of a man who ran travel tours for gay customers. Enforcement focuses on public expression and activism rather than private existence, and same-sex activity itself is not criminalised — a discreet visitor is not automatically targeted — but there is effectively no police protection, and detention carries placement by passport sex.

Chechnya and the wider North Caucasus, where quasi-Sharia governance applies, are in a separate and graver category of danger for anyone perceived as LGBT.

sources.claim: UK Home Office CPIN Russia: sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, updated Aug 2026): official country-of-origin information and assessment for asylum claims - the 'gay propaganda' laws, the 'extremist' designation of the 'international LGBT movement', the ban on legal/medical transition, and risk assessment.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for Russia (Level 4 'Do Not Travel') includes warnings relevant to LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch (Jun 2025): 'Russia: Rising Toll of LGBT ‘Extremism’ Designation' — documents raids, prosecutions and violence against LGBT people since the 'international LGBT public movement' was designated extremist.

Meduza feature (June 2025): 'What even is propaganda?' - how Russia's murky anti-LGBTQ laws fuel a repressive campaign that makes the state millions; cases under the 'LGBT propaganda' laws grew eighteenfold over a decade; fines in the past two years brought over 60 million rubles into state coffers; traces the law's evolution from 2013 (minors) to the December 2022 all-ages expansion.

The Moscow Times (June 2025): 'You're a second-class citizen' - arrests, club raids and extremism charges define LGBTQ life in Russia in 2025; since the Supreme Court declared the 'international LGBT movement' extremist, any public display of queerness (a rainbow badge, a photo with a same-sex partner, even a book) can be interpreted as extremist; unclear boundaries drive people to hide entirely.

AP (Dec 2024): 'Russian man arrested for allegedly running LGBTQ+ travel agency found dead in custody' — detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business, found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

AP (Dec 2024): 'Russia's LGBTQ+ community is living in fear following new laws and court rulings, activists say' — the post-designation crackdown under Putin pushes people into silence, flight and self-censorship.
Foreign Policy (Aug 2024): 'Russia's New Queer Purge: The Court Decision Driving the LGBT Community Into Exile' — how the extremism designation fuelled a purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians.

BBC Russian investigation (July 2024): 'Tricked into conversion therapy in Russia for being trans' - Ada, 23, was deceived into a Siberian 'conversion therapy centre' where she was held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and do manual labour, and told to castrate a pig to 'understand what castration means'; she escaped after nine months.

Novaya Gazeta Europe (June 2024): 'In limbo' - for many transgender Russians, emigration is the only means of survival after the law prohibiting gender-reassignment surgery and legal gender change; in 2023 one in three trans Russians said they had been threatened with physical violence (Coming Out/Sphere Foundation study).

The Guardian (Jan 2024): 'I will pretend not to be me' - Russia cracks down on the LGBTQ+ community; features queer performance artist Gena Marvin (documentary Queendom) challenging the Putin regime's gender norms through public performances.

records.name: Rwanda
records.summary:
Rwanda demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations). There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and civil society operates within the regime's tight limits.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex intimacy is not criminalised in Rwanda, but the Human Rights First Rwanda Association's 2025 UN submission highlighted law-enforcement abuses against trans people - harassment during identity checks and arbitrary arrests on 'vagrancy' or 'public order' grounds. Rainbow Migration reported in 2022 that Rwanda is 'now a source country' for people seeking UK asylum based on sexual orientation. LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly; activists held a public Pride event in 2023.

VICE World News (Nov 2020): 'Rwanda's Transgender Community Face Violent Detentions For Being Trans' - Bella, a singer, was detained by Kigali police on Christmas Day 2018 despite showing her work card; police falsely asserted she was homeless and sold drugs - documenting violent detentions of trans Rwandans.

KT Press (Sept 2016): President Kagame on LGBT life in Rwanda: 'it hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem'; Article 26 of the constitution recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman; Rwanda eliminated the criminalisation provision from its draft code in 2010 and signed two UN SOGI resolutions - the only African nation to do so.

The Queerstory Files (Oct 2012): 'Gay in the Great Lakes of Africa' - anthropologists say homosexuality was widespread among young men in both Tutsi and Hutu of pre-colonial Rwanda and Burundi, always private and secret - historical context for Rwanda.

records.name: Saudi Arabia
records.summary:
Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a transgender person to be discovered in. Under its uncodified Sharia legal system, same-sex conduct is punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment, and transgender expression itself is criminalised through "imitation of the opposite sex" and public-morality provisions that police and the morality police enforce with broad discretion. There is no legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care is banned.

Enforcement is documented and brutal: trans women have been arrested, detained, and tortured on morality grounds; a Pakistani trans woman died in custody in Riyadh in 2017 after a raid; men have been arrested for cross-dressing videos posted online. Amnesty International reported in 2026 that visitors have been imprisoned after unfair trials over social media posts — including posts published before they entered the Kingdom — and device inspection at the border is an established risk.

The tourism authority's "everyone is welcome" messaging reflects official interest in visitors' money, not any change in law. Any practical safety depends entirely on never being discovered, including digitally; detention would be in facilities matching passport sex, with no consular leverage able to prevent mistreatment.

sources.claim: LegalClarity overview (June 2026): Saudi Arabia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity - flogging, lengthy imprisonment and in the most severe cases death; no codified penal code (judges apply their own interpretation of Islamic law under the Basic Law of Governance); no protections, no relationship recognition, no gender-transition pathway; explains how the system works without a penal code and what visitors need to know.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): penalties based on Shariah with a maximum punishment of death; people suspected of homosexuality and trans women have been arrested, detained, tortured and prosecuted on morality grounds ('cross-dressing', 'offenses against Islam', 'attacks against public morals'); known executions for same-sex intimacy usually involve additional charges; in 2019 the state security agency published a video categorising feminism and homosexuality as 'extremist ideas' punishable by prison and flogging.

Cairo 52 country review of Saudi Arabia: deviation from traditional gender norms is a criminal offence under Sharia (social behaviour, medical interventions, surgical transition); no explicit legislation but arrests and severe punishments including corporal retribution are common; gender-affirming healthcare permitted only for intersex people; the Permanent Committee for Islamic Research rejects gender-affirming care and suggests prayer for gender dysphoria.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex activity illegal with capital punishment, indeterminate prison terms, flogging, fines and deportation; no gender-identity recognition; sections on enforcement cases, censorship, living conditions, and HIV/AIDS (including treatment of foreigners).

BBC (May 2017): the transgender tailor who died in Saudi custody - Pakistani trans elder Mohammad Amin ('Meeno Baji') was arrested at a party of transgender Pakistanis in Riyadh, thrown in Azizia prison, and died that night; Pakistani activists say he was beaten with clubs and hosepipes; Saudi authorities said he had a heart attack.

Gulf News (Oct 2021): five Saudi men arrested for cross-dressing - they filmed themselves walking the streets of the Northern Borders province and posted the video on social media; police said the conduct was 'inconsistent with the public morals of society'; criminal sanctions for cross-dressing mirror those for homosexuality (imprisonment, fines, deportation for foreigners).

Amnesty International/ALQST (June 2026, updated July 2026): visitors to Saudi Arabia - including tourists and Hajj/Umrah pilgrims - risk detention, grossly unfair trials and lengthy prison sentences for their social media activity, including posts published before entering the Kingdom; eight documented cases (July 2022 to late 2025), predominantly from Global South and Middle Eastern countries.

UK FCDO travel advice for Saudi Arabia: advises against all travel to parts and all but essential travel to other parts; safety and security, regional risks, pilgrimage guidance. General travel advice.

A3M Global Monitoring LGBTQ+ Risk Map 2025 (with Diversity Tourism and ITB Berlin): country dossiers assessing traveller risk on 80+ criteria; a world map assessing safety for LGBTQ+ travellers, with risk levels from 1 (low risk) upward, plus surveys and interviews with travel experts and community travellers.

The Guardian (April 2005) by Brian Whitaker: 'Saudis' tough line on gays' - dozens of Saudi men caught dancing and 'behaving like women' at a Jeddah party described as a 'gay wedding' were sentenced to a total of 14,200 lashes plus up to two years' jail, after a closed trial without defence lawyers; HRW's Scott Long: 'Prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct are flagrant human rights violations.'

records.name: Sudan
records.summary:
Sudan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Article 152 of the Penal Code criminalises gender nonconformity directly; sodomy carries life imprisonment (capital/corporal punishment removed in 2020 reforms); and Cairo 52 documents state violence against LGBTQIA+ people including extrajudicial killings. Since April 2023 the country has been in a catastrophic civil war (SAF vs RSF) with documented mass atrocities — the conflict intensifies every risk and eliminates any recourse. There is no LGR and no community infrastructure.

For a visitor: statutory criminalisation of gender nonconformity plus one of the world's worst active conflicts.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review of Sudan: Article 152 of the penal code criminalises gender nonconformity ('indecent' clothing - 40 lashes or a fine); documented state violence against LGBTQIA+ people including extrajudicial killings; gender-affirming healthcare constrained and no legal recognition; the ongoing conflict intensifies challenges; state reliance on Sunni fatwas obstructs transition.

Human Dignity Trust country profile: Sudan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with sentences including a maximum of life imprisonment (and historically the death penalty for a third offence). (Only the opening was retrievable at fetch time.)

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Sudan: documents the Bashir regime's abuses - extrajudicial killings, torture, Darfur conflict, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation under Article 148 with flogging and death penalty provisions.

Berkouwer, Sultan & Yehia (2014): 'Homosexuality in Sudan and Egypt: Stories of the Struggle for Survival' - by a Harvard research fellow with activists of Bedayaa (the LGBTQI organisation for the Nile Valley); explores daily struggles, discrimination and violence rooted in societal gender and sexual norms, and whether post-Arab-Spring change will transform circumstances.

Rainbow Sudan: 'Sudan's Magazine' - LGBTI rights in Sudan: history and analysis, organisation profile, and posts on regional LGBTI news and ancient-Egyptian sexuality - a Sudanese LGBTI community resource.

Erasing 76 Crimes (July 2020): Sudan dropped the death penalty for homosexuality - the Sovereign Council also eliminated 100 lashes, leaving up to 5 years for a first offence, 7 for a second, life for a third; Bedayaa hailed the reforms as 'a great step toward reforming the justice system' while Article 148 remains in force; only six nations then retained the death penalty for gay sex.

records.name: Senegal
records.summary:
Senegal is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “unnatural acts” (up to 5 years, applied to both men and women), enforcement is active (periodic arrest waves), and anti-LGBT forces are pushing to raise sentences to 15 years. Mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented, and even public discussion is policed: two men were jailed in 2024 for “false news” after accusing the Prime Minister of tolerating homosexuality. There is no legal gender recognition and no visible community infrastructure — Dakar's scene is deeply underground.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest and mob violence.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity (Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, up to 5 years' imprisonment). (Only the opening of the profile was retrievable at fetch time.)

Erasing 76 Crimes (July 2024): anti-LGBT forces in Senegal seek longer prison time - after PM Sonko alleged homosexuality is 'tolerated', MP Cheikh Abdou Bara Dolly Mbacké proposed a bill mirroring a failed 2022 initiative raising sentences to 10-15 years for 'offences of bisexuality [including homosexuality], transsexuality, necrophilia and zoophilia' plus fines up to 5 million CFA francs; abuses against LGBT+ people are commonplace.

BBC (June 2024): two men jailed in Senegal for 'spreading false news' after accusing PM Sonko of tolerating homosexuality - activist Bah Diakhate and Imam Ndao received three months and fines; Sonko had said homosexuality was 'not accepted, but tolerated' after a French politician expressed support for same-sex marriage at a Dakar student forum.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Senegal: documents preelectoral violence, torture, and 'violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons' among major human-rights problems.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Sept 2018): a wave of politically motivated anti-gay arrests as the 2019 election approached - two women and two men detained in Dakar for 'acts against the order of nature'; Arc en Ciel Senegal: 'The hunt for sexual minorities begins' as the government defends itself against 'pro-homosexual' accusations; Pan Africa ILGA called for accountability.
Metro (Nov 2023): a man's body was exhumed and set on fire in the street after locals found out he was gay - a case that shocked Senegal, where homosexuality is punishable with prison time.

records.name: Singapore
records.summary:
Singapore is broadly workable — far safer than its neighbour Malaysia, with no criminalisation of trans identity, no religious police, and one of the world's lowest crime rates. Section 377A (which criminalised sex between men) was repealed in 2022, and the prison service reports no assaults against its 10 transgender inmates — unusually positive for axis-H. Singapore is also a regional medical hub with gender-affirming care available.

The main gaps: legal gender recognition requires genital surgery (expensive and restrictive), there is no anti-discrimination law (the 2025 Workplace Fairness Act explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity), and over 65% of trans Singaporeans report negative workplace experiences. A radio code still groups homosexuality with "paedophilia and incest" as lifestyles barred from the airwaves. Progress has "stalled" since the 377A repeal, with discrimination "quietly tolerated."

For a visitor: efficient border processing, very low street crime, unrestricted bathrooms, and no trans-specific police friction. The atmosphere is conservative but quietly accommodating in practice.

sources.claim: TransgenderSG/Transbefrienders/NUS study 'Measuring Public Sentiments and Challenges Faced by Singapore's Transgender and Gender-Diverse Community' (Feb 2025): comprehensive survey covering demographics, school experiences, employment barriers and discrimination, healthcare access, gender-affirming care costs and experiences, and cisgender perspectives.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Section 377A repealed in 2022 (effective January 2023), but the constitution was simultaneously amended to codify marriage as between a man and a woman; adoption restrictions; trans people can change gender markers conditional on gender-affirming surgery; trans youth can access HRT with both parents' consent (16+ private, 18+ public), with much stricter access under 21.

Straits Times (Nov 2023): 10 transgender inmates behind bars in Singapore (one post-surgery, nine transitioning), with no assaults reported, per the Singapore Prison Service - raised in Parliament after the Scottish Isla Bryson case; housing arrangements discussed.

Pink Dot SG (Jan 2025): the new Workplace Fairness Legislation conspicuously and explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity - 'leaves the LGBTQ+ community empty-handed yet again'; a 2024 Pink Dot study found 69% of LGBTQ+ people encountered discrimination or harassment in hiring or at work; trans workers face some of the most severe discrimination including hiring barriers and safety threats.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature (June 2023) covers Singapore's LGBT community feeling safer as the end of the 377A ban brings change.

SCMP (July 2025): Singapore's radio broadcast code groups homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as 'lifestyles' not allowed on air - a former DJ and a blogger call for review, saying the clause 'has no place in post-377A Singapore'.
F&M Global Barometers country profile for Singapore: composite LGBT-rights perception scores including the Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.

Intrepid Travel country guide: LGBTQIA+ travellers to Singapore 'are welcomed and supported' though discretion with public displays of affection is recommended; notes Pink Dot rallies since 2009 and a gay-friendly bar scene.
